# Welcome {.unnumbered .unlisted}

This is the online version of **Reproducible Research for
the Health Sciences** by the rgtlab curriculum team, a graduate
course textbook.

In this book we take a position that any empirical
researcher will recognize from their own methodological
training.
[Computational reproducibility](glossary.qmd#gloss-computational-reproducibility)
is not a property of any
single file. It is a property of the relationships among
the operating system, the language runtime, the package
set, the session configuration, the source code, and the
data. A result reproduces when those relationships are
captured well enough that another person, on another
machine, at a later time, obtains the same answer. The
mature tools of the R ecosystem each capture one or two of
these relationships. The unsolved problem, and the subject
of this book, is composing them into a single workflow
that a working analyst can actually adopt.

We organize the book around three ideas that recur in
every chapter. The first is a ladder of reproducibility
levels. It runs from a merely locatable analysis (L0)
through pinned packages (L1) and a pinned environment (L2)
to a verified analysis whose recorded outputs have been
shown to regenerate (L3). The second is a distinction between
capturing reproducibility and validating it: pinning an
environment captures a level, whereas continuous
integration and [verification](glossary.qmd#gloss-verification)
confirm it. The third is the
[research compendium](glossary.qmd#gloss-research-compendium),
a single directory that bundles data,
code, and manuscript inside a structure that any reader can
navigate and any machine can rebuild.

The concrete vehicle throughout is `zzcollab`, an
open-source R framework built around the levels ladder and
written by the book's authors (the preface says more). It
composes the standard tools
([`renv`](glossary.qmd#gloss-renv-and-packrat) or Nix for packages,
Docker or a runtime alternative for the environment, a
research-compendium package structure, continuous
integration, testing, and data-integrity checking) into a
single system. We teach the concepts first and the tool
second. A reader who finishes the book should be able to
reason about reproducibility with any toolchain, and to
operate this one.

## Who the book is for

The reader we have in mind is a graduate student, often in
the first year, in any field that analyzes data to test
claims about the world. The health sciences, psychology,
economics, and ecology are examples. Such a reader
produces analyses that others will need to trust, audit,
and rebuild. The book's examples come from health research,
where the stakes of an analysis are easy to see, but the
principles apply to any empirical field.

## What the reader is assumed to know

- R from one course: running a script, installing a
  package, and reading a short function.
- Nothing about the command line, `git`, Docker, YAML,
  continuous integration, or Quarto. The
  [Shell Primer](shell-primer.qmd) takes a reader from a
  first terminal to the commands the book uses, and the
  [Setting Up Your Machine](setup-appendix.qmd) opens with a
  checklist of the software to install and how to confirm
  it works. Every other tool is built up from first
  principles in the chapter that needs it.
- Statistically, the ability to read a regression table
  and a confidence interval.

The first three chapters make the case for the practices
and need nothing beyond R itself. Work at the terminal
begins in @sec-version-control.
